records.place: Magill, Adelaide; Grange is drawn from across South Australia

wine.name: Grange
wine.grapes: Shiraz, the great majority, often with a small share of Cabernet Sauvignon.
wine.sites: No single site: Shiraz from several South Australian regions, the Barossa Valley above all, with McLaren Vale, the Clare Valley and, in some years, the Magill Estate vineyard in Adelaide.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tanks with header boards, or in open fermenters at Magill Estate, every component of the wine finishes its fermentation in new American oak hogsheads and then matures in them for seventeen to twenty months, by vintage, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and mulberry with liquorice, dark chocolate and the mocha and vanilla of new American oak; full in body and dense, with ripe, firm tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish with a graphite edge.
wine.ageing: Tight and oaky for its first ten years or so, it opens slowly; the house gives a strong vintage a drinking window that runs forty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The bin number Grange carries, a house code from the cellar rather than a legal classification.
The state appellation, wide enough to cover a blend from several of its regions.
The grape the label names; until the late 1980s the wine was sold as Grange Hermitage.

records.table: Penfolds Grange is a Shiraz blended from vineyards across South Australia rather than one site, finished in barrel and aged in new American oak. Dense, with blackberry, mocha and liquorice, it needs many years; decant it and pour it into a large glass.
records.story: Dr Christopher Rawson Penfold (1811 to 1870), an English physician, settled at Magill, east of Adelaide, in 1844 with his wife, and their stone cottage there, The Grange, would one day name the flagship. After his death in 1870 his wife ran the winery, and the house grew on fortified wine. In 1948 Max Schubert (1915 to 1994) became its first chief winemaker, and a visit to Bordeaux in 1950 set him on a red that could live for twenty years and more. He made the first Grange, experimentally, in 1951 from Shiraz grown at Magill and Morphett Vale; it was never sold. When senior management tasted the early vintages in 1957 they ordered him to stop, and he made the 1957, 1958 and 1959 in secret in the Magill cellars. Retasted with some age, the early wines changed the board's mind, and production resumed openly with the 1960 vintage. The wine was sold as Grange Hermitage, Hermitage being an old Australian name for Shiraz, until the late 1980s, and it has been made in every vintage since 1951. The house notes that South Australia lists it as a heritage icon. For a sommelier it is the standing answer to Henschke's Hill of Grace: one Shiraz blended across regions, the other grown on one hill.

others.name: Bin 389 Cabernet Shiraz
others.note: Matured in barrels that held the previous vintage of Grange, hence its nickname, Baby Grange.

others.name: St Henri Shiraz
others.note: Aged in large old vats with no new oak, the deliberate opposite of Grange in the cellar.

others.name: Bin 707 Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The Cabernet counterpart to Grange, also raised in new American oak.

traps: Grange is blended from several regions and many vineyards; Hill of Grace is the single vineyard Shiraz, made by Henschke in Eden Valley.
Grange Hermitage and Grange are one wine: Hermitage, an old Australian name for Shiraz, left the label in the late 1980s.
St Henri sees no new oak, so it is not a lesser Grange but its opposite in the cellar.

cards.front: Penfolds Grange: which three vintages did Max Schubert make in secret, and why?
cards.back: 1957, 1958 and 1959, in the Magill cellars, after senior management had ordered him to stop making the wine.

cards.front: Grange: in what oak does it mature, and where does its fermentation end?
cards.back: In American oak hogsheads, every one new, for seventeen to twenty months; the fermentation finishes in barrel.

questions.q: A guest asks why Penfolds Grange names no single vineyard on its label. Which answer is right?
opts: It is blended from vineyards across South Australia
It comes from one walled vineyard at Magill
Its vineyard is kept secret by the house
Australian law forbids naming a vineyard
questions.exp: Grange draws Shiraz from several regions, the Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale and the Clare Valley among them; the Magill Estate vineyard supplies some years beside them, never the whole wine.

questions.q: In 1957 Penfolds' senior management ordered Max Schubert to stop making Grange. What did he do?
opts: Made three vintages in secret in the Magill cellars
Took the idea to a rival house in the Barossa
Turned the Grange grapes into fortified wine
Waited until the board relented in 1965
questions.exp: Schubert made the 1957, 1958 and 1959 without approval in the Magill cellars; the board relented and production resumed openly with the 1960 vintage, not in 1965.

sources.title: Penfolds: Bin 95 Grange Shiraz 2021 tasting note

report: Every Penfolds page was read through search summaries; the facts of Grange's own history rest on the house's pages, with Wikipedia's page on Max Schubert and the library as the second sources.

The making now rests on the house's own words: partial barrel fermentation, every component finishing in new American oak hogsheads, stainless steel tanks with header boards at the Barossa winery and open fermenters at Magill, and 17, 18 or 20 months in barrel by vintage.
Penfolds' pages date Schubert's visit to Bordeaux to 1950, all but its 75th anniversary vertical page, which says 1949; the record keeps 1950.
Mary Penfold is described, not named: her death is 1895 in Penfolds' history and 1896 in Wikipedia's Penfolds article, and no source read gave her birth year.
One retailer's listing says Hermitage left the label with the 1990 vintage, the 1989 being the last Grange Hermitage; with a single source, the record keeps the library's late 1980s.
Schubert's last year as chief winemaker is 1975 in Penfolds' material and 1976 in Wikipedia's Penfolds article, so the record gives no end year.

The library's holdings line names Coonawarra among the regions; recent Grange notes name the Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale, the Clare Valley and Magill Estate, and Coonawarra appears in the 1990 blend, so sites gives examples, not a fixed list.

records.place: Keyneton, Eden Valley, Barossa, South Australia

wine.name: Hill of Grace
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from vines on their own roots.
wine.sites: The Hill of Grace vineyard near Keyneton, facing the Gnadenberg Lutheran church at about 400 metres; its oldest Shiraz, the Grandfathers, dates from about 1860, dry grown and ungrafted on red-brown earth over deep silty loam.
wine.making: Fermented in open fermenters, as the hand picked first vintage of 1958 was, the wine matures for eighteen to twenty months in oak hogsheads before blending and bottling; the barrels are mostly French and mostly seasoned rather than new, with a little American oak in some years.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and blueberry with five spice, star anise, sage and black pepper, and cedar from the barrel; perfumed rather than heavy, with velvety, fine-grained tannin, fresh acidity and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Worth leaving for several years after release, it gains savoury depth for decades; the house expects a well cellared bottle of a strong year to give pleasure for forty to fifty years.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or so, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The English for Gnadenberg, the name of the Lutheran church facing the vineyard, taken from a region of Silesia.
The higher, cooler region of the Barossa zone, an appellation of its own, separate from the Barossa Valley.

records.table: Henschke's Hill of Grace is Shiraz from one Eden Valley vineyard at Keyneton, facing the Gnadenberg church, where the oldest vines date from about 1860. Perfumed, with plum, five spice and sage over fine tannin, it is the single vineyard answer to Grange.
records.story: The family's founder, a stonemason and wheelwright from Silesia, reached South Australia in 1841, farmed first in the Adelaide Hills and at Krondorf, and then settled in the hills east of the Barossa Valley, in the district then called North Rhine and later Keyneton. He planted a small vineyard and made his first wine there in 1868. Close by, around 1860, a settler had planted Shiraz on land beside the Lutheran church of Gnadenberg, the Hill of Grace, and in 1891 the founder's son bought the land with its vines; he was the church's organist for many years. For decades the family made mostly fortified wine for sale in bulk. Cyril Henschke (1924 to 1979), of the fourth generation, turned the house towards dry table wine and towards wine of one vineyard: Mount Edelstone came first, and Hill of Grace followed with the 1958 vintage, hand picked and fermented in open vats. South Australia never had phylloxera, so the oldest block, the Grandfathers, grows on its own roots, and the vineyard came through the state's vine pull scheme of the 1980s, which took much of the Barossa's old Shiraz. After Cyril's death in 1979 the fifth generation took the house on. For a sommelier, Hill of Grace is the single vineyard half of the Barossa's standing pair, set against the blend of Grange.

others.name: Mount Edelstone
others.note: The house's other single vineyard Eden Valley Shiraz, from vines planted in 1912, bottled on its own before Hill of Grace.

others.name: Cyril Henschke Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The estate Cabernet, named for the man who made the first Hill of Grace.

others.name: Julius Eden Valley Riesling
others.note: Dry Riesling of lime and slate from the high country of Eden Valley.

traps: Hill of Grace is a vineyard name and carries no legal classification; it is not a Grand Cru.
Hill of Grace comes from Eden Valley, an appellation of its own, higher and cooler than the Barossa Valley floor.
Mount Edelstone, not Hill of Grace, was Henschke's first single vineyard Shiraz; Hill of Grace followed with the 1958 vintage.

cards.front: Hill of Grace: what is the Gnadenberg, and why does the wine carry its name?
cards.back: The Lutheran church that faces the vineyard; Gnadenberg means Hill of Grace, a name taken from a region of Silesia.

cards.front: Which Henschke made the first Hill of Grace, and with which vintage?
cards.back: Cyril Henschke (1924 to 1979), of the fourth generation, with the 1958 vintage.

questions.q: A guest asks why the oldest vines of Henschke's Hill of Grace grow on their own roots. Which answer fits?
opts: South Australia has never had phylloxera
The vineyard lies too high for any vine pest
The family regrafted them after the vine pull
Sandy soil there keeps phylloxera away
questions.exp: South Australia has kept phylloxera out, so vines planted around 1860 never needed grafting; the soil is red-brown earth over silty loam, not sand.

questions.q: In 1891 a son of Henschke's founder bought a vineyard planted around 1860 below a Lutheran church. What became of it?
opts: It became the Hill of Grace vineyard
It became the Mount Edelstone vineyard
It was pulled out in the 1980s vine pull
It became the site of the Keyneton winery
questions.exp: The vineyard by the Gnadenberg church is Hill of Grace, first bottled on its own with the 1958 vintage; Mount Edelstone is a separate vineyard, planted in 1912.

sources.title: Australian Dictionary of Biography: Cyril Alfred Henschke

report: The founder is described, not named: Wikipedia gives his birth in 1803, but no source read gave the year of his death.

Henschke's own history says he farmed first in the Adelaide Hills and bought land at Krondorf before the North Rhine land; Wikipedia dates the Keyneton purchase to 1862 and the house's page gives no year, so the story gives none.
The son who bought the vineyard in 1891 ran the Keyneton property from 1873, by the house's history, which calls him the second generation.

The planter of about 1860 was a forebear of the family by Henschke's account, and the ADB says Cyril Henschke's mother was born a Stanitzki; the story calls him a settler, since no dates for him were found.

The oak changes by vintage (2018: 18 months, a fifth new, mostly French with some American; 2021: 18 months, mostly seasoned French; 2022: 20 months, all seasoned French), so making gives the range, and hand picking is sourced for the first vintage only.
Mount Edelstone's first vintage is 1952 or 1953 by the house's count of seventy vintages in 2022, so the record says only that it came first, which the ADB and the house both support.
The say HENSH-kee is the common English say; no source of this run gives it, so a checker may empty it.

records.place: Krondorf Road, Tanunda, Barossa Valley, South Australia

wine.name: Basket Press Shiraz
wine.sites: Small parcels of old, dry grown Shiraz, most of them bought from grower families across the Barossa Valley, some of the vines more than a century old.
wine.making: Made on restored nineteenth century equipment, most of it salvaged as other cellars modernised: the fruit is fermented in open fermenters and pressed slowly and gently in a basket press more than a hundred years old, then matured in French and American oak hogsheads before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black plum and mulberry with dark chocolate, black pepper and a tarry, earthy note of forest floor; full in body, with velvety tannin from the gentle press and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight and tannic in its first years, it softens and gains depth over a decade or more in the cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an older one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: Pressed in an old basket press, the method the wine is named for, not a vineyard.
The appellation of the warm valley floor, as distinct from the higher Eden Valley.

records.table: Rockford's Basket Press Shiraz is old vine Barossa Valley Shiraz bought from grower families, fermented in open vats and pressed in a century old basket press. Full and velvety, with blackberry, chocolate and black pepper, it shows the Barossa as it was made before modern machinery.
records.story: Rockford grew from a property on Krondorf Road near Tanunda, bought by its founder in 1971, where a stone barn of the 1850s stands from the early settlement of Krondorf. The winery was put together from restored nineteenth century equipment, open fermenters and basket presses among it, much of it salvaged as other cellars modernised, and in 1984 the founder made the first Basket Press Shiraz; it has been made in every vintage since. The timing went against the market. In the mid 1980s, in a glut of grapes, the South Australian government paid growers to pull out their vines, and the Barossa lost much of its old Shiraz and Grenache. Rockford bought instead from the growers who had kept their old, dry grown vines, and built the house on its ties with those families more than on vines of its own. The wine became the traditionalist's Barossa Shiraz: slow basket pressing, open vats and a wine of texture rather than force. Its sparkling red, Black Shiraz, made by the traditional method, gave the house a second following. For a sommelier, Basket Press is the answer when a guest asks what Barossa Shiraz tasted like before new oak and heavy extraction became its fashion.

others.name: Black Shiraz
others.note: A sparkling red Shiraz made by the traditional method, dry to off dry, the house's other famous bottle.

others.name: Rod and Spur
others.note: A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, the classic Australian pairing.

traps: Rockford is not an estate: Basket Press comes mostly from growers' old vineyards, not from vines around the winery.
Black Shiraz is Rockford's sparkling red; Basket Press is a still Shiraz, and the two are different wines.
Basket Press names the press, not a vineyard and not a reserve level.

cards.front: Rockford Basket Press Shiraz: where does its fruit come from?
cards.back: Small parcels of old, dry grown Shiraz, most of them bought from Barossa grower families rather than grown on estate vines.

cards.front: In which year did Rockford make its first Basket Press Shiraz, and on what equipment?
cards.back: 1984, on restored nineteenth century equipment, open fermenters and basket presses among it, most of it salvaged from other cellars.

questions.q: A guest asks what the name Basket Press tells them about Rockford's Shiraz. Which answer is right?
opts: It is pressed slowly in an old basket press
It comes from a vineyard called Basket Press
It is a reserve level above the house Shiraz
It is fermented in baskets woven of vine canes
questions.exp: The name is the method: the wine is pressed gently and slowly in a basket press more than a century old; no vineyard and no reserve level is meant.

questions.q: In the mid 1980s, as Rockford began, what did the South Australian government pay Barossa growers to do?
opts: Pull out their vines
Graft their vines onto rootstock
Replant with Cabernet Sauvignon
Sell their fruit to cooperatives
questions.exp: The vine pull scheme paid growers to remove vines in a glut, and much old Shiraz and Grenache was lost; grafting was never needed, since the state has no phylloxera.

sources.title: J.J. Buckley: Realizing what Rockford is all about
Adelaide AZ: the Barossa Valley after the 1980s vine pull

report: Rockford's own host does not resolve from here, so the record rests on its visit page and Barossa Australia's listing read through search, with trade sources for the making and the first vintage.

The purchase of the Krondorf Road property in 1971 rests on trade profiles read as search summaries, which twice give 1971 while a cellar door listing says only the 1970s; no source disagrees, but the house's own site could not be read, so a checker should try the year again.
The library's style line says large old oak, but every source read says French and American oak hogsheads, so making says hogsheads; the library line may want the same change.
Sources date the vine pull scheme to 1985, 1986 or 1987, so the story says the mid 1980s.
Velvety is the house's own word for what the basket press gives; tasters call young vintages tannic, so ageing says tight in its first years.
The library's note that Basket Press is sold by allocation only, and any claim that it sells above all at the cellar door, are left out: both are volatile and neither was sourced.

wine.name: 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny
wine.grapes: Shiraz, Grenache or both, chosen parcel by parcel each year from the estate's own vineyards.
wine.sites: Barossa fruit; the wine is defined less by a vineyard than by the Centennial Cellar at Seppeltsfield, finished in 1878, where its cask rests for a century.
wine.making: Fermented and fortified with grape spirit while still sweet, as all the Para Tawnies are; a cask of each vintage is then laid down in the Centennial Cellar and left in wood for a hundred years, slowly concentrating, before it is bottled for release.
wine.glass: Treacle, walnut and burnt toffee with preserved fruit, exotic spice and the nutty tang of rancio; thick and intensely sweet, the sweetness held in check by concentration and a sharp volatile lift.
wine.ageing: Released ready to drink at a hundred years old; it needs no further cellaring.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, cool, as for an old tawny; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a small measure, after dinner.

label.means: The wine spent a century in its cask in the Centennial Cellar before release.
All of it comes from the one harvest named on the label, never a blend of years.
A sweet fortified wine aged in wood; Australian wine no longer carries the name Port.

records.table: Seppeltsfield's 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny is a fortified wine from a single Barossa harvest, released only after a century in cask in the Centennial Cellar. Treacle, walnut and toffee, thick and sweet, it is poured in small measures after dinner.
records.story: Joseph Ernst Seppelt (1813 to 1868), born in Lower Silesia, emigrated with his family to South Australia in 1849, and in 1851 he founded the estate in the Barossa Valley that took his name. He died suddenly in 1868, before the winery he had planned was complete, and his eldest son, still in his early twenties, took the business on and grew it. In 1878 the son completed the Centennial Cellar. That year he chose a puncheon of some five hundred litres of the estate's fortified wine and gave orders that it was not to be bottled for a hundred years. A cask from every vintage since has been laid down beside it, an unbroken line from 1878 to the present harvest. In 1978 the 1878 was released, a century old, and each year since the next vintage in the line has followed at a hundred years of age. When Australia agreed with the European Union to stop using the name Port, the house's Para wines went on as Tawny. For a sommelier it is history in a small glass: a wine laid down a century before it is poured, from a cellar where every year since 1878 waits its turn.

others.name: Para Grand Tawny
others.note: A younger, blended Para Tawny, the first step on the same ladder.

others.name: Para 21 Year Old Vintage Tawny
others.note: A single vintage released at twenty one years old, a younger rung of the same idea.

traps: Australian fortified wine no longer carries the name Port, a name of the Douro in Portugal; Tawny is the word on the label.
A 100 Year Old Para comes from one vintage, aged a century in its cask; it is not a blend whose wines average a hundred years.
The 1878, released in 1978, began the series; the Centennial Cellar holds a cask of every vintage since.

cards.front: Seppeltsfield's 100 Year Old Para: what happened in 1878, and in 1978?
cards.back: In 1878 a puncheon of that vintage was laid down in the new Centennial Cellar, not to be bottled for a century; in 1978 it was released.

cards.front: What does Vintage mean on a bottle of 100 Year Old Para Vintage Tawny?
cards.back: All of it comes from one named harvest, aged a century in its own cask, never a blend of years.

questions.q: A guest holding Seppeltsfield's 100 Year Old Para asks what the year on the label means. Which answer is right?
opts: The harvest every drop comes from
The average age of a blend of years
The year the bottle left the cellar
The year the Centennial Cellar was built
questions.exp: The wine of one harvest spends its century in cask and is released in its hundredth year, so the label's year is the harvest; the release comes a hundred years later.

questions.q: In 1878 the new Centennial Cellar at Seppeltsfield was completed. What was laid down in it that year?
opts: A puncheon not to be bottled for a century
The first Shiraz cuttings brought from Silesia
A solera begun from the founder's first harvest
The family's archive of labels and ledgers
questions.exp: The founder's son set aside a puncheon of the 1878 vintage with orders that it stay unbottled for a hundred years; it was released in 1978, and a cask of every vintage since has followed.

Australian Dictionary of Biography: Joseph Ernest Seppelt

report: The grapes rest on a retailer's listing of the 1923 release and a magazine interview, both read as search summaries: Shiraz, Grenache or both from the estate's own vineyards; the interview's move away from Mataro is left out for want of a date, and no source read gives the grapes of the old vintages now released.

The library's advanced question a-l68ugdzs in js/data-advanced.js calls Seppeltsfield's treasure an unbroken Para tawny solera begun in 1878; it is no solera but one cask of each single vintage, kept apart, as the house's timeline and every source read describe it, and the question's explanation wants that word changed.
The founder's son is described, not named: the ADB gives his birth as 1845 and Wikipedia as 1846.
Serve follows the Codex's service reference for tawny, 10 to 14 degrees Celsius, not a figure from the house.
The house counts the 1926 its 49th consecutive release while one listing calls the 1919 the 41st, which does not reconcile, so the record gives no count.
Rancio, preserved fruit and exotic spice are the house's words on its Centennial Cellar page and its 1926 release page, read through search; treacle, walnut and burnt toffee are the library's.

wine.name: The Signature Cabernet Sauvignon Shiraz
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, the share of each changing with the vintage.
wine.sites: Barossa vineyards, with Shiraz from vines planted as early as 1945; the first vintage, 1962, joined Eden Valley Shiraz to Cabernet Sauvignon from the house's Oxford Landing vineyard.
wine.making: Matured for eighteen to twenty two months, by vintage, in hogsheads and barriques of French and Hungarian oak, with American oak in some earlier vintages and a fifth or so of the barrels new in recent ones; the first vintage was raised in French puncheons. The house runs its own cooperage.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, blackberry and plum with smoke and a savoury note of grilled meat; the Cabernet gives a frame of firm, fine tannin and the Shiraz flesh in the middle, with a long, dry finish.
wine.ageing: Closed and firm for its first years, it is made to cellar and opens slowly over a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Each vintage is dedicated to one person who has given much to Yalumba, its Signatory.
The zone appellation, which covers both the Barossa Valley floor and the higher Eden Valley.
The two grapes of the blend, a pairing Australia has long made its own.

records.table: Yalumba's The Signature is a Barossa blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, made since 1962 and dedicated each vintage to one person who has served the house. Blackcurrant and plum over firm Cabernet tannin, it is built to cellar, so decant a young bottle.
records.story: Samuel Smith (1812 to 1889), a brewer from Wareham in Dorset, brought his wife and five children to South Australia in 1847 and by 1849 was working as a gardener at Angaston. That year he bought land of his own and named it Yalumba, by most accounts an Aboriginal word for all the land around; the story goes that he planted his first vines by moonlight, after his day's work on his employer's estate. The house traces itself to that planting and has stayed with his descendants, which makes it, by its own account, Australia's oldest family owned winery, and it keeps its own cooperage. The Signature began with the 1962 vintage, a blend of Eden Valley Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon matured in French puncheons, and was first released in 1966. Each vintage is dedicated to one person who has given much to Yalumba, members of its staff among them, and more than fifty have been honoured so far. The blend has moved with the vineyards: the modern wine is drawn from the Barossa and raised in French and Hungarian oak. For a sommelier it is the Cabernet Shiraz blend, a pairing Australia made its own, told through one family house and the people who served it.

others.name: The Octavius
others.note: Old vine Barossa Shiraz aged in octaves, small American oak casks made in the house's own cooperage.

others.name: The Virgilius
others.note: Eden Valley Viognier, from a grape the house has long championed.

others.name: Pewsey Vale The Contours Riesling
others.note: Dry Eden Valley Riesling of lime, released with bottle age.

traps: The Signature blends Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz; it is not a single varietal Shiraz like The Octavius.
The Signature's first vintage was 1962, but that wine was not released until 1966.
An octave is a small cask, not a vineyard or a blend term.

cards.front: Yalumba's The Signature: what does its name refer to?
cards.back: Each vintage is dedicated to one person who has given much to the house, its Signatory; more than fifty have been honoured since 1962.

cards.front: What went into the first vintage of Yalumba's The Signature, the 1962?
cards.back: Eden Valley Shiraz and Cabernet Sauvignon from the Oxford Landing vineyard, matured in French puncheons; it was released in 1966.

questions.q: A guest asks what sets Yalumba's The Signature apart from a Barossa Shiraz. Which answer is right?
opts: It blends Cabernet Sauvignon with Shiraz
It is Shiraz from a single Eden Valley block
It is aged only in large old vats
It is a fortified red of the Barossa
questions.exp: The Signature is a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Shiraz, the share of each changing with the vintage; it is raised in hogsheads and barriques, not old vats, and is a dry table wine.

questions.q: Samuel Smith founded Yalumba at Angaston in 1849. What had been his trade in England?
opts: Brewer
Physician
Stonemason
Cooper
questions.exp: Smith was a brewer from Wareham in Dorset; the Penfolds founder was the physician, and Henschke's founder the stonemason and wheelwright.

Australian Dictionary of Biography: Samuel Smith

report: One retailer's page says The Signature grew out of a Special Reserve Galway Claret of 1942, rebadged in 1962; the house's own pages make 1962 the first vintage and 1966 the first release, and the record follows the house.
The oak changes by vintage (2005: 22 months, French, American and Hungarian, 31 per cent new; 2022: 18 months; 2023: 19 months, 22 per cent new, French and Hungarian), so making gives the range.

Smith's arrival is August 1847 in Wikipedia and December 1847 in SA Memory, and the ADB's life summary gives Morden for his birthplace where its biography says Wareham; the record keeps the year and Wareham, which the biography and Wikipedia share.
The house counted more than 57 Signatories on its 2023 page, so more than fifty is a floor that stays true.
The house's newer red, The Caley, could be argued as its flagship today; The Signature is kept for its sixty years of history, and no swap is proposed.
